# The pipeline, re-run and timed — 2026-09-13

## Access and confidence

One machine, one afternoon: Apple M4, 24 GB, macOS, Node 22.22.3, ffmpeg
from Homebrew, the finance video project as committed (`video/fixed-or-variable`,
`hyperframes@0.8.33` pinned, `kokoro-onnx` 0.4.7 in its venv). Each step
was run once, alone, with a browser and an editor open. Order of magnitude,
not the value.

## `check` — 16 s

`npx --yes hyperframes@0.8.33 check`: lint, then the browser pass — runtime,
layout, motion, and 26 of 26 text elements passing WCAG AA contrast. It also
said the pin lags the latest release (0.8.33 against 0.8.36).

## `tts` — 8.6 s of speech in 9.7 s, download included

`npx --yes hyperframes@0.8.33 tts "<two sentences, 30 words>" -v af_heart -o /tmp/tts-test.wav`

The voice file was not cached on this machine and the command fetched it
first ("Downloading voice data (~27 MB)"), then synthesised 8.6 s of audio;
9.7 s wall in all. The output is a 24 kHz mono WAV — the ai-planning README
says 44.1 kHz; it is 24. What Kokoro keeps on disk, in
`~/.cache/hyperframes/tts/`: the model `kokoro-v1.0.onnx`, **324 MB**, and
`voices-v1.0.bin`, 28 MB. The "~27 MB model" in the READMEs is the voices
file; the model is twelve times that.

## `render` — 100 s of video in 2 min 10 s

`npx --yes hyperframes@0.8.33 render -o /tmp/fov-rerender.mp4 --crf 23 --low-memory-mode`

The trace: 3,013 frames, `workerCount: 1`, `captureMode: screenshot`,
`forceScreenshot: true` — the safe profile the flag's help text describes
(one worker, screenshot capture, no calibration). "4.3 MB · 1m 40.4s video ·
rendered in 2m 9.7s"; 135 s wall including the CLI's own start-up. Output:
1920 × 1080, H.264 at 30 fps, AAC audio, 100.43 s.

**Not byte-identical.** The shipped file is 4,554,529 bytes; the re-render
4,554,482 — 47 bytes apart, different MD5. HyperFrames promises that the
same timestamp resolves to the same frame, and nothing in the difference
suggests otherwise; but the H.264 encoder does not promise the same bytes
from run to run, and a rendered MP4 is not something to diff. Compare
frames, or durations, or watch it.

## What the numbers say

- A 100-second narrated explainer renders in about the time it takes to
  watch it, on one worker, on a laptop, with the safe profile on. The
  default profile (auto-calibrated workers, fast capture on a macOS GPU)
  would be faster; it was not measured, because the project's own README
  says the safe profile is what worked here.
- Narration is far faster than real time once the 352 MB of model and
  voices are cached: the two sentences took about a second after the
  download.
- The check is the cheap step. Sixteen seconds is less than one preview.
